why: The old solution quoted r=(s-a)tan(A/2) as a result to be taken on trust; the rewrite derives it from equal tangent lengths and the right triangle at A. Separately, note for the source ledger: the data is geometrically impossible (A=60 with a=2 caps the perimeter at 6, and b+c=8 with bc=20 has non-real roots), so this is a formula drill on an inconsistent triangle - the arithmetic is unambiguous and still yields the keyed value.
solution:
The semiperimeter is \(s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}=\dfrac{10}{2}=5\) cm, so \(s-a=5-2=3\) cm.

Let the incircle touch \(BC, CA, AB\) at \(D, E, F\). Tangents drawn to a circle from an external point are equal, so \(AE=AF=x\), \(BF=BD=y\), \(CD=CE=z\). Then \(x+y=c\), \(y+z=a\) and \(z+x=b\); adding these gives \(2(x+y+z)=a+b+c=2s\), so \(x+y+z=s\) and therefore \(AF=x=s-(y+z)=s-a=3\) cm.

The incentre \(I\) lies on the bisector of \(\angle A\), and \(IF\perp AB\), so triangle \(AFI\) is right-angled at \(F\) with \(\angle FAI=\dfrac{A}{2}\), \(AF=s-a\) and \(IF=r\). Hence \(\tan\dfrac{A}{2}=\dfrac{r}{s-a}\), that is \(r=(s-a)\tan\dfrac{A}{2}\).

With \(A=60^\circ\), \(\tan\dfrac{A}{2}=\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(r=3\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}\) cm.

Hence (A).

why: The old solution broke off mid-step, handed the work to the source, and its quoted intermediate radicand was wrong; the rewrite computes the parameter, the foot and the distance in full.
solution:
The line passes through \(A(-3,\,4,\,-8)\) with direction \(\vec{d}=(3,\,5,\,6)\), and the given point is \(P(-2,\,4,\,-5)\).

First, \(\vec{AP}=(-2+3,\;4-4,\;-5+8)=(1,\,0,\,3)\).

Let the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) be \(B=A+\lambda\vec{d}\). Then \(\vec{PB}=B-P=\lambda\vec{d}-\vec{AP}\), and \(\vec{PB}\cdot\vec{d}=0\) gives \(\lambda\,|\vec{d}|^{2}=\vec{AP}\cdot\vec{d}\).

Here \(\vec{AP}\cdot\vec{d}=1(3)+0(5)+3(6)=21\) and \(|\vec{d}|^{2}=9+25+36=70\), so \(\lambda=\dfrac{21}{70}=\dfrac{3}{10}\).

Therefore \(\vec{PB}=\dfrac{3}{10}(3,\,5,\,6)-(1,\,0,\,3)=\left(\dfrac{9}{10}-1,\;\dfrac{3}{2}-0,\;\dfrac{9}{5}-3\right)=\left(-\dfrac{1}{10},\;\dfrac{3}{2},\;-\dfrac{6}{5}\right)\).

\(|\vec{PB}|^{2}=\dfrac{1}{100}+\dfrac{9}{4}+\dfrac{36}{25}=\dfrac{1+225+144}{100}=\dfrac{370}{100}=\dfrac{37}{10}\).

So the required distance is \(\sqrt{\dfrac{37}{10}}\).

Hence (C).

why: The old solution mis-parametrised the second line (it used x-3=2r instead of x-3=2r-2), reached k=-0.5, and then simply deferred to the source for 9/2; the rewrite parametrises both lines correctly and lands on 9/2.
solution:
Put \(\dfrac{x-1}{2}=\dfrac{y+1}{3}=\dfrac{z-1}{4}=r\), so a general point of the first line is \((1+2r,\;-1+3r,\;1+4r)\).

Put \(\dfrac{x-3}{1}=\dfrac{y-k}{2}=\dfrac{z}{1}=s\), so a general point of the second line is \((3+s,\;k+2s,\;s)\).

The lines meet when all three coordinates agree.

From the \(z\)-coordinates: \(1+4r=s\).

From the \(x\)-coordinates: \(1+2r=3+s=3+(1+4r)=4+4r\), so \(-3=2r\) and \(r=-\dfrac{3}{2}\). Then \(s=1+4\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)=1-6=-5\).

From the \(y\)-coordinates: \(-1+3r=k+2s\), so \(-1+3\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)=k+2(-5)\), that is \(-\dfrac{11}{2}=k-10\), giving \(k=10-\dfrac{11}{2}=\dfrac{9}{2}\).

With \(k=\dfrac{9}{2}\), the first line at \(r=-\dfrac{3}{2}\) gives \(\left(-2,\;-\dfrac{11}{2},\;-5\right)\), and the second at \(s=-5\) gives \(\left(-2,\;\dfrac{9}{2}-10,\;-5\right)=\left(-2,\;-\dfrac{11}{2},\;-5\right)\) - the same point, so the lines do intersect.

Hence (C).

why: The old solution trailed off into a question mark and then concluded option B (c.a=|b|^2), contradicting the keyed option D; the rewrite eliminates A, B and C by orthogonality and proves D with the vector triple product.
solution:
Since \(\vec{b}=\vec{c}\times\vec{a}\), the vector \(\vec{b}\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{c}\) and \(\vec{a}\), so \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=0\) and \(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=0\). Since \(\vec{c}=\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\), the vector \(\vec{c}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{a}\), so \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}=0\).

So option A would require \(|\vec{c}|^{2}=0\), option B would require \(|\vec{b}|^{2}=0\) and option C would require \(|\vec{a}|^{2}=0\); all three fail for non-zero vectors.

For option D, substitute \(\vec{b}=\vec{c}\times\vec{a}\) and apply the vector triple product identity \((\vec{u}\times\vec{v})\times\vec{w}=(\vec{u}\cdot\vec{w})\vec{v}-(\vec{v}\cdot\vec{w})\vec{u}\) with \(\vec{u}=\vec{c}\), \(\vec{v}=\vec{a}\), \(\vec{w}=\vec{c}\):

\(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=(\vec{c}\times\vec{a})\times\vec{c}=(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{c}=|\vec{c}|^{2}\vec{a}-0\cdot\vec{c}=|\vec{c}|^{2}\vec{a}\).

So \(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\) is a scalar multiple of \(\vec{a}\), which means \(\vec{a}\parallel(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\).

Hence (D).

why: The old solution said the substitution 'simplifies to' the answer without performing a single cross product; the rewrite expands both terms.
solution:
From \(2\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+\vec{c}=\vec{0}\) we get \(\vec{a}=-\dfrac{3\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{2}\).

Cross with \(\vec{b}\):
\(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(3\vec{b}+\vec{c}\right)\times\vec{b}=-\dfrac{3}{2}\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{b}\right)-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\vec{c}\times\vec{b}\right)=\vec{0}+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)\),
using \(\vec{b}\times\vec{b}=\vec{0}\) and \(\vec{c}\times\vec{b}=-\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)\).

Cross \(\vec{c}\) with \(\vec{a}\):
\(\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\,\vec{c}\times\left(3\vec{b}+\vec{c}\right)=-\dfrac{3}{2}\left(\vec{c}\times\vec{b}\right)-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\vec{c}\times\vec{c}\right)=\dfrac{3}{2}\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)-\vec{0}=\dfrac{3}{2}\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)\).

Adding the three terms:
\(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}+\vec{b}\times\vec{c}+\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+1+\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)=3\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution wrote down the determinant and then asserted the answer as a result to be taken on trust; the rewrite expands the determinant and carries out the substitution x=1-a, y=1-b, z=1-c that produces the identity.
solution:
The three vectors are coplanar exactly when their scalar triple product vanishes, that is when the determinant of their components is zero. Expanding along the first row:

\(a(bc-1)-1(c-1)+1(1-b)=0\)

\(abc-a-c+1+1-b=0\), so \(abc-a-b-c+2=0\).

Now put \(x=1-a\), \(y=1-b\), \(z=1-c\); each is non-zero because \(a,b,c\ne 1\). Then \(a=1-x\), \(b=1-y\), \(c=1-z\), and

\(abc=(1-x)(1-y)(1-z)=1-(x+y+z)+(xy+yz+zx)-xyz\),

\(a+b+c=3-(x+y+z)\).

Substituting into \(abc-(a+b+c)+2=0\):

\(\left[1-(x+y+z)+(xy+yz+zx)-xyz\right]-\left[3-(x+y+z)\right]+2=0\).

The constants give \(1-3+2=0\) and the terms \(-(x+y+z)\) and \(+(x+y+z)\) cancel, leaving

\(xy+yz+zx-xyz=0\), that is \(xy+yz+zx=xyz\).

Dividing throughout by \(xyz\neq 0\):

\(\dfrac{1}{z}+\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{y}=1\), that is \(\dfrac{1}{1-a}+\dfrac{1}{1-b}+\dfrac{1}{1-c}=1\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution simply quoted the tangent equation as a result to be memorised; the rewrite obtains the slope by implicit differentiation and derives the equation.
solution:
Differentiate \(y^{2}=4ax\) with respect to \(x\): \(2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4a\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2a}{y}\).

At the point \(\left(at^{2},\,2at\right)\) we have \(y=2at\), so the slope of the tangent is \(\dfrac{2a}{2at}=\dfrac{1}{t}\).

The tangent through \(\left(at^{2},\,2at\right)\) with this slope is

\(y-2at=\dfrac{1}{t}\left(x-at^{2}\right)\).

Multiplying both sides by \(t\):

\(ty-2at^{2}=x-at^{2}\), so \(ty=x-at^{2}+2at^{2}=x+at^{2}\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution asserted that the incident slope 'works out to' 41/38 without any reflection computation; the rewrite reflects a point of the reflected ray in the mirror line, finding the foot of the perpendicular explicitly.
solution:
Both given lines pass through the meeting point: \(7(0)-1+1=0\) and \(2(0)+1=1\), so the mirror line \(7x-y+1=0\) and the reflected ray \(2x+y=1\) both pass through \((0,\,1)\).

The incident ray is the mirror image of the reflected ray in the line \(7x-y+1=0\), so it is enough to reflect one point of the reflected ray. Take \(M(1,\,-1)\), which lies on \(2x+y=1\) since \(2(1)+(-1)=1\).

The mirror has slope \(7\), so the perpendicular from \(M\) to it has slope \(-\dfrac{1}{7}\):

\(y+1=-\dfrac{1}{7}(x-1)\), that is \(7y+7=-x+1\), or \(x+7y+6=0\).

The mirror gives \(y=7x+1\). Substituting: \(x+7(7x+1)+6=0\Rightarrow 50x+13=0\Rightarrow x=-\dfrac{13}{50}\), and \(y=7\left(-\dfrac{13}{50}\right)+1=-\dfrac{91}{50}+\dfrac{50}{50}=-\dfrac{41}{50}\).

So the foot of the perpendicular is \(N\left(-\dfrac{13}{50},\,-\dfrac{41}{50}\right)\), and \(N\) is the midpoint of \(M\) and its image \(M'\). Therefore

\(M'=2N-M=\left(-\dfrac{26}{50}-1,\;-\dfrac{82}{50}+1\right)=\left(-\dfrac{76}{50},\;-\dfrac{32}{50}\right)=\left(-\dfrac{38}{25},\;-\dfrac{16}{25}\right)\).

The line of incidence joins \((0,\,1)\) and \(M'\), so its slope is

\(\dfrac{-\dfrac{16}{25}-1}{-\dfrac{38}{25}-0}=\dfrac{-\dfrac{41}{25}}{-\dfrac{38}{25}}=\dfrac{41}{38}\).

Its equation is \(y-1=\dfrac{41}{38}x\), that is \(38y-38=41x\), or \(41x-38y+38=0\).

Hence (C).

why: The old text skipped the whole separable integration and then stated option D's expression while naming option B, so it contradicted itself.
solution:
The right side depends on \(y/x\), so put \(y=vx\), giving \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\).

Substituting: \(v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=v+x\sin v\), so \(x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=x\sin v\), i.e. \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\sin v\).

Separate the variables: \(\dfrac{dv}{\sin v}=dx\), so \(\int\csc v\,dv=\int dx\), which gives \(\log\left|\tan\dfrac{v}{2}\right|=x+k\).

Exponentiating, \(\tan\dfrac{v}{2}=Ce^{x}\) where \(C=\pm e^{k}\). Hence \(\dfrac{v}{2}=\tan^{-1}(Ce^{x})\), so \(v=2\tan^{-1}(Ce^{x})\).

Restoring \(v=\dfrac{y}{x}\): \(\dfrac{y}{x}=2\tan^{-1}(Ce^{x})\), that is \(y=2x\tan^{-1}(Ce^{x})\).

Hence (B).

why: The old text asserted that an integrating factor makes the left side the derivative of \(y\log|x|\) without ever applying the product rule to show it.
solution:
Apply the product rule to \(y\log|x|\):
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(y\log|x|\big)=\log|x|\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}=\log|x|\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{y}{x}\),
which is exactly the left-hand side of the equation.

So the equation reads \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(y\log|x|\big)=\sin 2x\).

Integrate both sides with respect to \(x\), using \(\int\sin 2x\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\):
\(y\log|x|=C-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\).

Hence (C).

why: The old text quoted the value as a named result and only parenthesised the method instead of carrying out the substitution and evaluating the limits.
solution:
Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^2x\):
\(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sec^2x}{a^2\tan^2x+b^2}\,dx\).

Put \(t=\tan x\), so \(dt=\sec^2x\,dx\). The limits become \(x=0\Rightarrow t=0\) and \(x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^{-}\Rightarrow t\to\infty\):
\(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{a^2t^2+b^2}=\frac{1}{a^2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{t^2+\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{2}}\).

Using \(\int\dfrac{dt}{t^2+c^2}=\dfrac{1}{c}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{c}\) with \(c=\dfrac{b}{a}\):
\(I=\dfrac{1}{a^2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{b}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{at}{b}\right]_{0}^{\infty}=\dfrac{1}{ab}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-0\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{2ab}\).

Hence (C).

why: The old text named the reflection property but never performed the substitution, so the cancellation that produces \(2I\) was never shown.
solution:
First simplify the integrand: \(\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\cos x}=1+\tan x\), so
\(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log(1+\tan x)\,dx\).

Apply \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)\,dx\) with \(a=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Since \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x\right)=\dfrac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}\),
\(1+\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x\right)=1+\dfrac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}=\dfrac{(1+\tan x)+(1-\tan x)}{1+\tan x}=\dfrac{2}{1+\tan x}\).

Therefore
\(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log\frac{2}{1+\tan x}\,dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log 2\,dx-\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\log(1+\tan x)\,dx=\frac{\pi}{4}\log 2-I\).

So \(2I=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\log 2\), giving \(I=\dfrac{\pi}{8}\log 2\).

Hence (D).

why: The old text quoted the value as a named result and its parenthetical sketch was internally inconsistent, jumping from \(2I=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2\) to \(I=-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2\).
solution:
Let \(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin x)\,dx\).

By \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)\,dx\) with \(a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), and \(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\cos x\):
\(I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\cos x)\,dx\).

Add the two expressions for \(I\):
\(2I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin x\cos x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\,dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin 2x)\,dx-\frac{\pi}{2}\log 2\).

In the remaining integral put \(t=2x\), \(dt=2\,dx\):
\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin 2x)\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi}\log(\sin t)\,dt\).

Since \(\sin(\pi-t)=\sin t\), the integrand is symmetric about \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\log(\sin t)\,dt=2\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin t)\,dt=2I\). Hence \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin 2x)\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2I=I\).

Substituting back: \(2I=I-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2\), so \(I=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2\).

Hence (D).

why: The old text said to integrate by parts twice but performed neither pass, so the reader never sees where the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) comes from.
solution:
Put \(x=e^{t}\), so \(\log x=t\) and \(dx=e^{t}\,dt\):
\(I=\displaystyle\int\cos(\log x)\,dx=\int e^{t}\cos t\,dt\).

Integrate by parts with \(u=\cos t\), \(dv=e^{t}dt\):
\(I=e^{t}\cos t+\displaystyle\int e^{t}\sin t\,dt\).

Integrate \(\displaystyle\int e^{t}\sin t\,dt\) by parts again with \(u=\sin t\), \(dv=e^{t}dt\):
\(\displaystyle\int e^{t}\sin t\,dt=e^{t}\sin t-\int e^{t}\cos t\,dt=e^{t}\sin t-I\).

Substituting this back: \(I=e^{t}\cos t+e^{t}\sin t-I\), so \(2I=e^{t}(\cos t+\sin t)\) and
\(I=\dfrac{e^{t}}{2}(\cos t+\sin t)+c\).

Restoring \(e^{t}=x\) and \(t=\log x\):
\(F(x)=\dfrac{x}{2}\big[\cos(\log x)+\sin(\log x)\big]\).

Differentiating this back confirms it: \(F'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\big[\cos(\log x)+\sin(\log x)\big]+\dfrac{x}{2}\left[\dfrac{-\sin(\log x)}{x}+\dfrac{\cos(\log x)}{x}\right]=\cos(\log x)\).

Hence (C).

why: The old text asserted the normal "works out to" \(x+y=2\sqrt{2}\), and the point it printed was wrong — the parameter term is \(\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\), not \(\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}\).
solution:
Differentiate the parametric equations:
\(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-2\sin t+2\sin t+2t\cos t=2t\cos t\),
\(\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2\cos t-2\cos t+2t\sin t=2t\sin t\).

So \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2t\sin t}{2t\cos t}=\tan t\), and the normal has slope \(-\cot t\).

At \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) the slope of the normal is \(-\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=-1\), and the point of contact is
\(x_{0}=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2+\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}\),
\(y_{0}=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2-\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}\).

The normal is \(y-y_{0}=-1\cdot(x-x_{0})\), i.e. \(x+y=x_{0}+y_{0}\). The two \(\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}\) terms cancel, leaving \(x_{0}+y_{0}=2\sqrt2\), so the normal is
\(x+y-2\sqrt2=0\).

Its distance from the origin is \(\dfrac{|0+0-2\sqrt2|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}}=\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=2\).

Hence (C).

why: The old text set up the differentiated equation and then jumped straight to the answer, hiding the entire algebraic cancellation that is the whole point of the question.
solution:
Take logarithms of \(x^{m}y^{n}=(x+y)^{m+n}\):
\(m\log x+n\log y=(m+n)\log(x+y)\).

Differentiate with respect to \(x\), writing \(y'=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\):
\(\dfrac{m}{x}+\dfrac{n}{y}\,y'=\dfrac{(m+n)(1+y')}{x+y}\).

Gather the \(y'\) terms on the right:
\(\dfrac{m}{x}-\dfrac{m+n}{x+y}=y'\left[\dfrac{m+n}{x+y}-\dfrac{n}{y}\right]\).

Combine each side over a common denominator.
Left: \(\dfrac{m(x+y)-(m+n)x}{x(x+y)}=\dfrac{mx+my-mx-nx}{x(x+y)}=\dfrac{my-nx}{x(x+y)}\).
Bracket on the right: \(\dfrac{(m+n)y-n(x+y)}{y(x+y)}=\dfrac{my+ny-nx-ny}{y(x+y)}=\dfrac{my-nx}{y(x+y)}\).

So \(\dfrac{my-nx}{x(x+y)}=y'\cdot\dfrac{my-nx}{y(x+y)}\).

Cancelling the common factor \(\dfrac{my-nx}{x+y}\) leaves \(\dfrac{1}{x}=\dfrac{y'}{y}\), that is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{x}\).

Hence (D).

why: The old text quoted the ratio as a named result rather than deriving it, so nothing explains where \(m\) and \(n\) come from.
solution:
Both numerator and denominator vanish at \(x=1\), so divide each by \(x-1\):
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^{m}-1}{x^{n}-1}=\lim_{x\to1}\frac{\dfrac{x^{m}-1}{x-1}}{\dfrac{x^{n}-1}{x-1}}\).

Each piece is a difference quotient at \(x=1\): for any exponent \(k\),
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^{k}-1}{x-1}=\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^{k}-1^{k}}{x-1}=\left.\frac{d}{dx}x^{k}\right|_{x=1}=\left.kx^{k-1}\right|_{x=1}=k\).

So the numerator tends to \(m\) and the denominator to \(n\); since \(n\neq0\), the quotient of the limits gives
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^{m}-1}{x^{n}-1}=\frac{m}{n}\).

Hence (B).

why: The derivation itself was sound but it closed by citing a numerical spot-check as justification; the rewrite keeps the argument and replaces that citation with the exact evaluations, which are already the real evidence.
solution:
\(\tan A=\cot B\) means \(\tan A=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-B\right)\), so \(A=n\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}-B\), i.e. \(A+B=n\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

Here \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\theta=n\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), which gives \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=2n+1\).

Since \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\sin\left(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\) lies in \([-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]\) and \(2n+1\) is an odd integer, the only possibilities are \(2n+1=1\) and \(2n+1=-1\).

Case \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=1\): \(\sin\left(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), so \(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}=2r\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) or \(2r\pi+\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\), giving \(\theta=2r\pi\) or \(\theta=2r\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). At \(\theta=2r\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) we have \(\sin\theta=1\), and \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is undefined, so that branch is rejected. At \(\theta=2r\pi\): \(\sin\theta=0\) gives \(\tan 0=0\), and \(\cos\theta=1\) gives \(\cot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=0\) — both sides equal \(0\), so it is a solution.

Case \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=-1\): \(\sin\left(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), giving \(\theta=2r\pi+\pi\) or \(\theta=2r\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). The second has \(\sin\theta=-1\), and \(\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is undefined, so it is rejected. At \(\theta=2r\pi+\pi\): \(\sin\theta=0\) gives \(\tan 0=0\), and \(\cos\theta=-1\) gives \(\cot\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0\) — again both sides are \(0\), so it is a solution.

The complete solution set is therefore \(\theta=2r\pi\) together with \(\theta=2r\pi+\pi\), that is \(\theta=r\pi,\ r\in Z\) — every integer multiple of \(\pi\), not only the even ones.

Option (B) lists only \(\theta=2r\pi\) and omits the odd multiples, so it is incomplete. Options (A) and (C) include \(\theta=2r\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), where both sides are undefined. No listed option is the full solution set.

Hence (D).

why: The old text said only "working through" and then cited a numerical check; neither \(x^{2}+y^{2}\) nor \(x^{2}-y^{2}\) was ever computed.
solution:
First, \(\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^{2}\theta}=\tan 2\theta\), so the three equal quantities are \(x\sin\theta\), \(y\cos\theta\) and \(z\tan2\theta\).

Let their common value be \(K\). Then
\(x=\dfrac{K}{\sin\theta}\), \(y=\dfrac{K}{\cos\theta}\), \(z=\dfrac{K}{\tan2\theta}=K\cot2\theta\).

Now, using \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) so that \(\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta=\dfrac{\sin^{2}2\theta}{4}\):
\(x^{2}+y^{2}=K^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}\right)=K^{2}\cdot\dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta}=\dfrac{K^{2}}{\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta}=\dfrac{4K^{2}}{\sin^{2}2\theta}\).

Similarly, using \(\cos^{2}\theta-\sin^{2}\theta=\cos2\theta\):
\(x^{2}-y^{2}=K^{2}\cdot\dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta-\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta}=\dfrac{4K^{2}\cos2\theta}{\sin^{2}2\theta}\).

Therefore
\(4z^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})=4K^{2}\cot^{2}2\theta\cdot\dfrac{4K^{2}}{\sin^{2}2\theta}=\dfrac{16K^{4}\cos^{2}2\theta}{\sin^{2}2\theta\cdot\sin^{2}2\theta}=\dfrac{16K^{4}\cos^{2}2\theta}{\sin^{4}2\theta}\),
while
\((x^{2}-y^{2})^{2}=\left(\dfrac{4K^{2}\cos2\theta}{\sin^{2}2\theta}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{16K^{4}\cos^{2}2\theta}{\sin^{4}2\theta}\).

The two expressions are the same, so \(4z^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})=(x^{2}-y^{2})^{2}\).

Hence (C).

why: The old text named the recurrence and asserted the answer without ever writing out the two substitutions, so the telescoping cancellation was invisible.
solution:
Start from the identity
\(\cot\theta-\tan\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}-\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta-\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\dfrac{\cos2\theta}{\frac{1}{2}\sin2\theta}=2\cot2\theta\),
which rearranges to \(\tan\theta=\cot\theta-2\cot2\theta\).

With \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{5}\): \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{5}=\cot\dfrac{\pi}{5}-2\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\).

With \(\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\): \(\tan\dfrac{2\pi}{5}=\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{5}-2\cot\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\), so \(2\tan\dfrac{2\pi}{5}=2\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{5}-4\cot\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\).

Add these to the third term:
\(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{5}+2\tan\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+4\cot\dfrac{4\pi}{5}=\left(\cot\dfrac{\pi}{5}-2\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)+\left(2\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{5}-4\cot\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\right)+4\cot\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\).

The \(\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\) terms cancel and so do the \(\cot\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\) terms, leaving \(\cot\dfrac{\pi}{5}\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution set up 16(m^2-n^2) and 16mn and then jumped to the conclusion with "working through" plus a numerical check; the sum-and-difference step that actually closes it was never shown.
solution:
Read the two givens as a sum and a difference.
\(4m + 4n = \cot\theta[(1+\sin\theta)+(1-\sin\theta)] = 2\cot\theta\), so \(m+n = \dfrac{\cot\theta}{2}\).
\(4m - 4n = \cot\theta[(1+\sin\theta)-(1-\sin\theta)] = 2\cot\theta\sin\theta = 2\cos\theta\), since \(\cot\theta\sin\theta = \cos\theta\); so \(m-n = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{2}\).
Hence \(m^2-n^2 = (m+n)(m-n) = \dfrac{\cot\theta\cos\theta}{4}\), and squaring, \((m^2-n^2)^2 = \dfrac{\cot^2\theta\cos^2\theta}{16}\).
Now the product of the two givens: \(16mn = \cot^2\theta(1+\sin\theta)(1-\sin\theta) = \cot^2\theta(1-\sin^2\theta) = \cot^2\theta\cos^2\theta\), so \(mn = \dfrac{\cot^2\theta\cos^2\theta}{16}\).
The two right-hand sides are the same expression, so \((m^2-n^2)^2 = mn\). Hence (A).

why: The old solution named the half-angle formula and then said "after simplification" without performing the substitution, so the factorisation that produces the answer was invisible.
solution:
Use the half-angle formula \(\tan^2\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}\) and substitute the given \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\cos\alpha-\cos\beta}{1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta}\).
Numerator:
\(1-\cos\theta = \dfrac{(1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta)-(\cos\alpha-\cos\beta)}{1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta} = \dfrac{(1+\cos\beta)-\cos\alpha(1+\cos\beta)}{1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta} = \dfrac{(1+\cos\beta)(1-\cos\alpha)}{1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta}\).
Denominator:
\(1+\cos\theta = \dfrac{(1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta)+(\cos\alpha-\cos\beta)}{1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta} = \dfrac{(1-\cos\beta)+\cos\alpha(1-\cos\beta)}{1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta} = \dfrac{(1-\cos\beta)(1+\cos\alpha)}{1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta}\).
Dividing, the factor \(1-\cos\alpha\cos\beta\) cancels:
\(\tan^2\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1-\cos\alpha}{1+\cos\alpha}\cdot\dfrac{1+\cos\beta}{1-\cos\beta} = \tan^2\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\cdot\cot^2\dfrac{\beta}{2}\),
using \(\tan^2\dfrac{\alpha}{2} = \dfrac{1-\cos\alpha}{1+\cos\alpha}\) and \(\cot^2\dfrac{\beta}{2} = \dfrac{1+\cos\beta}{1-\cos\beta}\).
Taking square roots, \(\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \pm\,\cot\dfrac{\beta}{2}\tan\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\), so one of the values is \(\cot\dfrac{\beta}{2}\tan\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\). Hence (A).

why: The old solution had the right two identities but never accounted for how the n twos are distributed between the innermost multiplier and the outer layers, which is the whole point of the question, and leaned on a numerical check instead.
solution:
Innermost layer: \(2(1+\cos\theta) = 4\cos^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}\) by the identity \(1+\cos\phi = 2\cos^2\dfrac{\phi}{2}\), so \(\sqrt{2(1+\cos\theta)} = 2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\) — the positive root, because \(0^\circ<\theta<180^\circ\) places \(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\) in the first quadrant where the cosine is positive.
Every outer layer repeats the same step: \(\sqrt{2+2\cos\phi} = \sqrt{4\cos^2\dfrac{\phi}{2}} = 2\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}\), which halves the angle each time.
Count the twos: one of them is the multiplier inside the innermost radical, so the remaining \(n-1\) are the outer \(2+\) terms. The innermost radical gives \(2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), and the \(n-1\) outer layers halve that angle \(n-1\) further times, giving
\(2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2^{\,1+(n-1)}} = 2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2^{n}}\).
The two smallest cases confirm the indexing: for \(n=1\) the expression is \(\sqrt{2(1+\cos\theta)} = 2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), and for \(n=2\) it is \(\sqrt{2+2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}} = 2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{4}\). Hence (A).

why: The old solution miscounted the conditioning event — it called the denominator 5 entities when tying the 4 American couples still leaves the Indian man and his wife as two separate people (6 entities) — and then asserted the ratio rather than dividing.
solution:
Ten people sit round a circle. Condition on the given event: each of the four American men is next to his wife.
Denominator. Tie each American couple into a single block. The circle then holds those 4 blocks plus the Indian man and the Indian wife as two separate people — 6 entities. Six entities can be arranged round a circle in \((6-1)! = 120\) ways, and each of the 4 blocks can be internally ordered in 2 ways, so the number of seatings satisfying the condition is \(120\times 2^4 = 1920\).
Numerator. Now require in addition that the Indian man sits next to his wife. All 5 couples are then blocks — 5 entities — arranged round the circle in \((5-1)! = 24\) ways, each of the 5 blocks internally ordered in 2 ways: \(24\times 2^5 = 24\times 32 = 768\) seatings.
Conditional probability \(= \dfrac{768}{1920} = \dfrac{2}{5}\). Hence (C).

why: The old solution wrote down the determinant condition and the product \((1+a)(1+b)(1+c)\) but never combined them — it said "one finds" and appealed to a numerical check, hiding the one line that makes the answer exact.
solution:
A homogeneous system has a non-trivial solution exactly when its coefficient determinant is zero:
\(\begin{vmatrix} a & a & -1 \\ b & -1 & b \\ -1 & c & c \end{vmatrix} = a(-c-bc) - a(bc+b) - (bc-1) = -2abc - ab - bc - ca + 1 = 0\),
that is, \(ab+bc+ca+2abc = 1\).   ...(i)
Now put \(S = \dfrac{1}{1+a}+\dfrac{1}{1+b}+\dfrac{1}{1+c}\) over the common denominator \((1+a)(1+b)(1+c)\). Writing \(p=a+b+c\), \(q=ab+bc+ca\), \(r=abc\):
numerator \(= (1+b)(1+c)+(1+a)(1+c)+(1+a)(1+b) = 3 + 2p + q\),
denominator \(= (1+a)(1+b)(1+c) = 1 + p + q + r\).
Subtract twice the denominator from the numerator:
\((3+2p+q) - 2(1+p+q+r) = 1 - q - 2r\),
and by (i) \(q + 2r = 1\), so this difference is exactly 0.
Therefore numerator \(= 2\times\) denominator, i.e. \(S = 2\). Hence (C).

why: Two steps were asserted rather than done — the algebra collapsing the AP condition to \(n^2-9n+14=0\), and the claim that the odd-power coefficients sum to \(2^{n-1}\).
solution:
In \((1+x)^n\) the general term is \(T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r}x^r\), so the 2nd, 3rd and 4th coefficients are \(\binom{n}{1}, \binom{n}{2}, \binom{n}{3}\) (a 4th term requires \(n\ge 3\)).
AP condition (middle term is the average of its neighbours):
\(2\binom{n}{2} = \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{3}\), i.e. \(2\cdot\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = n + \dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}\), so \(n(n-1) = n + \dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}\).
Divide by \(n\) (\(n>0\)): \(n-1 = 1 + \dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{6}\).
Multiply by 6: \(6n-6 = 6 + (n-1)(n-2) = 6 + n^2 - 3n + 2\), so \(n^2 - 9n + 14 = 0\), i.e. \((n-2)(n-7) = 0\). Since \(n=2\) leaves no 4th term, \(n = 7\).
Sum of the coefficients of odd powers: put \(x=1\) in \((1+x)^7\) to get \(\sum_r \binom{7}{r} = 2^7\), and put \(x=-1\) to get \(\sum_r (-1)^r\binom{7}{r} = 0\). Subtracting the second from the first cancels every even-power coefficient and doubles every odd-power one, so twice the required sum is \(2^7 - 0\), giving \(2^6 = 64\). Hence (B).

why: The old solution stated the G.P. condition and then jumped straight to the answer in one asserted step — the entire computation converting the condition into the two cotangent powers was missing.
solution:
G.P. condition (square of the middle term equals the product of the outer two):
\(\cos^2\theta = \sin\theta\tan\theta = \sin\theta\cdot\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}\),
so \(\cos^3\theta = \sin^2\theta\).   ...(i)
Use (i) to express the two powers of \(\cot\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\) alone. Cubing (i) gives \(\sin^6\theta = \cos^9\theta\), hence
\(\cot^6\theta = \dfrac{\cos^6\theta}{\sin^6\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^6\theta}{\cos^9\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos^3\theta}\),
\(\cot^2\theta = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos^3\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\).
Subtract:
\(\cot^6\theta - \cot^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos^3\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1-\cos^2\theta}{\cos^3\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^3\theta}\),
and by (i) the numerator equals the denominator, so the value is \(1\). Hence (A).

why: The evaluations were right but the solution ended by deferring to the source and to "the bank state" rather than standing on its own reasoning; the underlying stem is defective (statement 2 has lost its "= 0"), so the rewrite states the literal reading that supports the key without appealing to any outside authority.
solution:
\(f(x) = x^2 - 3\) is an even function, so \(f(-1) = f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2\). Continuing the iteration, \(f(-2) = 4 - 3 = 1\) and \(f(1) = -2\).
Therefore \((f\circ f\circ f)(1) = f\big(f(f(1))\big) = f\big(f(-2)\big) = f(1) = -2\), and by the same chain \((f\circ f\circ f)(-1) = f\big(f(-2)\big) = f(1) = -2\). The two agree, so statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2 carries no equality, inequality or claim of any kind: it is the bare expression \((f\circ f\circ f)(-1) - 4(f\circ f\circ f)(1) - (f\circ f)(0)\). Its value is
\(-2 - 4(-2) - f(f(0)) = -2 + 8 - f(-3) = 6 - (9-3) = 6 - 6 = 0\),
but an expression asserts nothing, so there is no proposition in statement 2 that can be judged correct.
Only statement 1 is correct. Hence (A).

why: The old solution multiplied \(\sqrt3/8\) by 2 with no explanation and then appealed to an unnamed product formula; neither the pairing nor the triple-angle step was shown.
solution:
In degrees, \(\dfrac{\pi}{18} = 10^\circ\), \(\dfrac{5\pi}{18} = 50^\circ\), \(\dfrac{7\pi}{18} = 70^\circ\), so \(K = \sin 10^\circ\,\sin 50^\circ\,\sin 70^\circ\).
Pair the last two, writing \(50^\circ = 60^\circ - 10^\circ\) and \(70^\circ = 60^\circ + 10^\circ\), and apply the identity \(\sin(A-B)\sin(A+B) = \sin^2 A - \sin^2 B\):
\(\sin 50^\circ\sin 70^\circ = \sin^2 60^\circ - \sin^2 10^\circ = \dfrac{3}{4} - \sin^2 10^\circ\).
Therefore
\(K = \sin 10^\circ\left(\dfrac{3}{4} - \sin^2 10^\circ\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(3\sin 10^\circ - 4\sin^3 10^\circ\right)\).
The bracket is the triple-angle identity \(\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta\) at \(\theta = 10^\circ\), so it equals \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
Hence \(K = \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{8}\). Hence (C).

why: The question IS the identity \(\operatorname{adj}(A^T) = (\operatorname{adj}A)^T\), so citing it as a known fact makes the solution circular; the entry-by-entry proof is three lines and is what the question is testing.
solution:
Write \(C_{ij}(A)\) for the cofactor of the \((i,j)\) entry of \(A\), so that by definition \((\operatorname{adj}A)_{ij} = C_{ji}(A)\) — the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
Deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\) of \(A^T\) leaves precisely the transpose of what remains after deleting row \(j\) and column \(i\) of \(A\), and a determinant is unchanged by transposition, so the minors satisfy \(M_{ij}(A^T) = M_{ji}(A)\). The sign \((-1)^{i+j}\) is symmetric in \(i\) and \(j\), so \(C_{ij}(A^T) = C_{ji}(A)\).
Now compare the two matrices entry by entry:
\(\big(\operatorname{adj}A^T\big)_{ij} = C_{ji}(A^T) = C_{ij}(A)\),
\(\big((\operatorname{adj}A)^T\big)_{ij} = (\operatorname{adj}A)_{ji} = C_{ij}(A)\).
Every entry matches, so \(\operatorname{adj}A^T = (\operatorname{adj}A)^T\) and their difference is the zero matrix. Since \(A\) is \(n\times n\), its adjoint is \(n\times n\), so the difference is the null matrix of the same order as \(A\). Hence (C).

why: The old solution expanded the determinant and then invoked the answer as a known fact; the step joining the coplanarity condition to the sum of the three fractions was never taken.
solution:
Three vectors are coplanar exactly when their scalar triple product vanishes:
\(\begin{vmatrix} a & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & b & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & c \end{vmatrix} = a(bc-1) - (c-1) + (1-b) = abc - a - b - c + 2 = 0\).   ...(i)
Put \(S = \dfrac{1}{1-a}+\dfrac{1}{1-b}+\dfrac{1}{1-c}\) over the common denominator \((1-a)(1-b)(1-c)\), which is non-zero because \(a,b,c \neq 1\):
numerator \(= (1-b)(1-c) + (1-a)(1-c) + (1-a)(1-b)\)
\(= (1-b-c+bc) + (1-a-c+ac) + (1-a-b+ab) = 3 - 2(a+b+c) + (ab+bc+ca)\),
denominator \(= (1-a)(1-b)(1-c) = 1 - (a+b+c) + (ab+bc+ca) - abc\).
Subtract the denominator from the numerator; the \((ab+bc+ca)\) terms cancel and the linear terms combine:
numerator \(-\) denominator \(= 2 - (a+b+c) + abc\),
which is exactly the left-hand side of (i) and is therefore 0.
So the numerator equals the denominator and \(S = 1\). Hence (B).

why: The old solution started one counting route, abandoned it mid-sentence with 'Actually', started a second route, and then jumped to the printed figure without ever multiplying anything out.
solution:
Side I has 8 chairs and must contain the 4 particular men; side II has 8 chairs and must contain the 2 particular men. That leaves \(16-4-2=10\) unrestricted people, of whom \(8-4=4\) must go to side I and \(8-2=6\) to side II.

Step 1 — split the 10 unrestricted people. Choose which 4 of them sit on side I:
\(\binom{10}{4}=\dfrac{10\times 9\times 8\times 7}{4\times 3\times 2\times 1}=\dfrac{5040}{24}=210\) ways.
The remaining 6 go to side II, so no further choice is needed.

Step 2 — seat each side. Side I now has a fixed set of 8 people and 8 distinct chairs, giving \(8!\) arrangements; side II likewise gives \(8!\) arrangements.

Total \(=210\times 8!\times 8!\).

Hence (C).

why: The old solution wrote two broken half-finished fractions with trailing dots, then asserted the product equals s/(s-b) without deriving it.
solution:
From \(a-2b+c=0\) we get \(a+c=2b\), so
\(s=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}=\dfrac{2b+b}{2}=\dfrac{3b}{2}\), and \(s-b=\dfrac{3b}{2}-b=\dfrac{b}{2}\).

Now use the half-angle formulas \(\tan\dfrac{A}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(s-b)(s-c)}{s(s-a)}}\) and \(\tan\dfrac{C}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(s-a)(s-b)}{s(s-c)}}\). Taking reciprocals,
\(\cot\dfrac{A}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s(s-a)}{(s-b)(s-c)}}\) and \(\cot\dfrac{C}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s(s-c)}{(s-a)(s-b)}}\).

Multiply the two, and the factors \((s-a)\) and \((s-c)\) cancel between numerator and denominator:
\(\cot\dfrac{A}{2}\cot\dfrac{C}{2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s(s-a)}{(s-b)(s-c)}\cdot\dfrac{s(s-c)}{(s-a)(s-b)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s^{2}(s-a)(s-c)}{(s-a)(s-c)(s-b)^{2}}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{s^{2}}{(s-b)^{2}}}=\dfrac{s}{s-b}\).

Substituting the two values found above:
\(\cot\dfrac{A}{2}\cot\dfrac{C}{2}=\dfrac{3b/2}{b/2}=3\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution named a column operation that does not produce the claimed structure, said 'Vandermonde-like', and then asserted the answer without expanding or fixing the sign.
solution:
Observe that every row sums to 1: \((1-\alpha)+(\alpha-\alpha^{2})+\alpha^{2}=1\), and likewise for the \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) rows.

Step 1 — apply \(C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3\) (this leaves the determinant unchanged). Every entry of the first column becomes 1:
\(\begin{vmatrix}1 & \alpha-\alpha^{2} & \alpha^{2}\\ 1 & \beta-\beta^{2} & \beta^{2}\\ 1 & \gamma-\gamma^{2} & \gamma^{2}\end{vmatrix}\)

Step 2 — apply \(C_2\to C_2+C_3\). The second column becomes \(\alpha-\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{2}=\alpha\), and similarly \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\):
\(\begin{vmatrix}1 & \alpha & \alpha^{2}\\ 1 & \beta & \beta^{2}\\ 1 & \gamma & \gamma^{2}\end{vmatrix}\)

Step 3 — expand this Vandermonde determinant. Do \(R_2\to R_2-R_1\) and \(R_3\to R_3-R_1\):
\(\begin{vmatrix}1 & \alpha & \alpha^{2}\\ 0 & \beta-\alpha & \beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}\\ 0 & \gamma-\alpha & \gamma^{2}-\alpha^{2}\end{vmatrix}\)
Expanding along the first column and factoring \((\beta-\alpha)\) out of \(R_2\) and \((\gamma-\alpha)\) out of \(R_3\), using \(\beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta+\alpha)\):
\(=(\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)\begin{vmatrix}1 & \beta+\alpha\\ 1 & \gamma+\alpha\end{vmatrix}=(\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)\big[(\gamma+\alpha)-(\beta+\alpha)\big]=(\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)(\gamma-\beta)\).

Step 4 — match the option form. Flip the sign of two factors: \((\beta-\alpha)=-(\alpha-\beta)\) and \((\gamma-\beta)=-(\beta-\gamma)\). The two minus signs cancel:
\((\beta-\alpha)(\gamma-\alpha)(\gamma-\beta)=(-1)(\alpha-\beta)\cdot(\gamma-\alpha)\cdot(-1)(\beta-\gamma)=(\alpha-\beta)(\beta-\gamma)(\gamma-\alpha)\).

Hence (B).

why: The inequality argument was sound, but it was framed as adopting whichever reading of the stem makes the paper's answer come out right; the ordering in fact needs only 0<P(A)<P(B)<1, so the ratio never enters.
solution:
Write \(p=P(A\cap B)\). The three quantities being compared are
\(P(A\cap B)=p\), \(\quad P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{p}{P(B)}\), \(\quad P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{p}{P(A)}\),
all with the same numerator \(p\), so the ordering is decided entirely by the denominators. Take \(p>0\); if \(p=0\) all three are 0 and no strict ordering exists.

First comparison. Since \(0<P(B)<1\), dividing the positive number \(p\) by \(P(B)\) enlarges it:
\(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{p}{P(B)}>\dfrac{p}{1}=p=P(A\cap B)\).

Second comparison. Since \(0<P(A)<P(B)\), taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses the inequality: \(\dfrac{1}{P(A)}>\dfrac{1}{P(B)}\). Multiplying through by \(p>0\):
\(P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{p}{P(A)}>\dfrac{p}{P(B)}=P(A\mid B)\).

Chaining the two:
\(P(A\cap B)<P(A\mid B)<P(B\mid A)\).

[Note: only \(0<P(A)<P(B)<1\) was used. The stem's ratio condition \(2P(A)=3P(B)\) would give \(P(A)=\tfrac{3}{2}P(B)>P(B)\), which conflicts with \(P(A)<P(B)\); since the ratio plays no part in either comparison above, the ordering is unaffected either way.]

Hence (D).

why: The old solution hid the squaring algebra behind 'Squaring and simplifying gives'; the half-angle route below avoids squaring altogether, so no extraneous roots are created in the first place.
solution:
Use \(1+\cos x=2\cos^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\) and \(\sin x=2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\):
\(\csc x+\cot x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}+\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\dfrac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}=\dfrac{2\cos^{2}\frac{x}{2}}{2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}}=\dfrac{\cos\frac{x}{2}}{\sin\frac{x}{2}}=\cot\dfrac{x}{2}\).
This is valid wherever \(\sin x\neq 0\), which the original equation already requires.

So the equation becomes \(\cot\dfrac{x}{2}=\sqrt{3}\).

For \(0<x<2\pi\) we have \(0<\dfrac{x}{2}<\pi\), and \(\cot\) is strictly decreasing on \((0,\pi)\), so it attains the value \(\sqrt{3}\) exactly once there. Since \(\cot\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\sqrt{3}\), that point is \(\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), i.e. \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

Substituting back: \(\csc\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\cot\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}\), so it satisfies the equation.

The other listed values fail: at \(x=\pi\), \(\sin x=0\), so \(\csc x\) and \(\cot x\) are undefined; at \(x=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\), \(\csc x=-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(\cot x=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), whose sum is \(-\sqrt{3}\neq\sqrt{3}\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution wrote down the discriminant of g and then tagged '(can be shown)' onto the one claim the whole question turns on — that it is negative — without expanding it.
solution:
Let \(f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c\). For \(f\) to be positive for every real \(x\) it must open upwards and never meet the axis, so
\(a>0\) and \(b^{2}-4ac<0\).

Differentiate: \(f'(x)=2ax+b\) and \(f''(x)=2a\). Therefore
\(g(x)=(ax^{2}+bx+c)+(2ax+b)+2a=ax^{2}+(b+2a)x+(c+b+2a)\),
again a quadratic, with the same leading coefficient \(a>0\).

Now expand its discriminant term by term:
\((b+2a)^{2}-4a(c+b+2a)=b^{2}+4ab+4a^{2}-4ac-4ab-8a^{2}\).
The \(4ab\) terms cancel and \(4a^{2}-8a^{2}=-4a^{2}\), leaving
\(=b^{2}-4ac-4a^{2}=(b^{2}-4ac)-4a^{2}\).

Both pieces are negative: \(b^{2}-4ac<0\) by hypothesis, and \(-4a^{2}<0\) because \(a\neq 0\). So the discriminant of \(g\) is strictly negative.

A quadratic with positive leading coefficient and negative discriminant has no real zero, so it never changes sign and never reaches 0; its sign is that of its leading coefficient. Hence \(g(x)>0\) for every real \(x\) — strictly, so the weaker option \(g(x)\geq 0\) is not the sharpest true statement.

Hence (B).

why: The old solution reached the condition b^2/(ac)=q^2/(pr) and then jumped straight to the answer with '(can be shown via the ratio condition)', skipping the cancellation that is the entire point.
solution:
Let the roots of \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\) be \(\alpha,\beta\) in the ratio \(k:1\), and the roots of \(px^{2}+qx+r=0\) be \(\gamma,\delta\) in the same ratio \(k:1\).

Step 1 — turn the ratio into a coefficient relation. For the first equation \(\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}\) and \(\alpha\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}\), so
\(\dfrac{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}}{\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{b^{2}/a^{2}}{c/a}=\dfrac{b^{2}}{ac}\).
Writing the roots as \(\alpha=kt,\ \beta=t\), the same expression is
\(\dfrac{(kt+t)^{2}}{kt\cdot t}=\dfrac{t^{2}(k+1)^{2}}{kt^{2}}=\dfrac{(k+1)^{2}}{k}\).
So \(\dfrac{b^{2}}{ac}=\dfrac{(k+1)^{2}}{k}\), and by the identical argument \(\dfrac{q^{2}}{pr}=\dfrac{(k+1)^{2}}{k}\).

Step 2 — call this common value \(m\), so \(ac=\dfrac{b^{2}}{m}\) and \(pr=\dfrac{q^{2}}{m}\). Substitute into the discriminants:
\(D_{1}=b^{2}-4ac=b^{2}-\dfrac{4b^{2}}{m}=b^{2}\cdot\dfrac{m-4}{m}\),
\(D_{2}=q^{2}-4pr=q^{2}-\dfrac{4q^{2}}{m}=q^{2}\cdot\dfrac{m-4}{m}\).

Step 3 — divide. The factor \(\dfrac{m-4}{m}\) is the same in both and cancels (it is non-zero precisely when \(D_{2}\neq 0\), i.e. \(k\neq 1\), which the division requires anyway):
\(\dfrac{D_{1}}{D_{2}}=\dfrac{b^{2}\cdot\frac{m-4}{m}}{q^{2}\cdot\frac{m-4}{m}}=\dfrac{b^{2}}{q^{2}}\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution named the reversal law and gestured at one product without associating the factors, and never said why uniqueness of the inverse lets you conclude from it.
solution:
Since \(A\) and \(B\) are invertible, \(A^{-1}\) and \(B^{-1}\) exist. Multiply \(AB\) by the candidate \(B^{-1}A^{-1}\) on each side, regrouping by associativity:

\((AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=A\,I\,A^{-1}=AA^{-1}=I\),

\((B^{-1}A^{-1})(AB)=B^{-1}(A^{-1}A)B=B^{-1}\,I\,B=B^{-1}B=I\).

So \(B^{-1}A^{-1}\) is a two-sided inverse of \(AB\). The inverse of a matrix is unique, therefore \((AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

The order cannot be swapped: \((AB)(A^{-1}B^{-1})=A(BA^{-1})B^{-1}\), and \(BA^{-1}\) does not collapse to \(I\) unless \(A\) and \(B\) happen to commute.

Hence (A).

why: The old solution quoted A·adj(A)=det(A)I as a bare result with no reason; the cofactor-expansion argument for it is two lines and belongs in the answer.
solution:
Let \(A=[a_{ij}]\) be of order \(n\) and let \(C_{ij}\) denote the cofactor of \(a_{ij}\). By definition the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, so \(B=\mathrm{adj}(A)\) has \((i,j)\) entry \(C_{ji}\).

The \((i,j)\) entry of \(AB\) is therefore
\((AB)_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^{n}a_{it}\,C_{jt}\).

Diagonal entries \((i=j)\): \(\sum_{t}a_{it}C_{it}\) is exactly the cofactor expansion of \(\det A\) along row \(i\), so \((AB)_{ii}=\det A=k\).

Off-diagonal entries \((i\neq j)\): \(\sum_{t}a_{it}C_{jt}\) is the cofactor expansion along row \(j\) of the matrix obtained from \(A\) by replacing row \(j\) with a copy of row \(i\) — the cofactors \(C_{jt}\) do not involve row \(j\), so they are unchanged by that replacement. That matrix has two identical rows (rows \(i\) and \(j\)), so its determinant is 0, giving \((AB)_{ij}=0\).

So \(AB\) carries \(k\) all along its diagonal and 0 everywhere else, that is \(AB=kI\), written \(kl\) in the options.

Hence (B).

why: The old solution asserted a formula for cos(alpha-beta) carrying an unexplained square root of ambiguous sign, then hid the whole cancellation behind 'substituting and simplifying gives'.
solution:
Put \(u=\theta-\alpha\) and \(v=\theta-\beta\), so that \(\cos u=a\) and \(\cos v=b\). Then
\(\alpha-\beta=(\theta-\beta)-(\theta-\alpha)=v-u\).

Step 1 — expand the cosine of the difference:
\(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos(v-u)=\cos v\cos u+\sin v\sin u=ab+s\), where \(s=\sin u\sin v\).

Step 2 — record what \(s^{2}\) is (its sign is never needed):
\(s^{2}=\sin^{2}u\,\sin^{2}v=(1-\cos^{2}u)(1-\cos^{2}v)=(1-a^{2})(1-b^{2})=1-a^{2}-b^{2}+a^{2}b^{2}\).

Step 3 — write \(c=\cos(\alpha-\beta)=ab+s\), so \(\sin^{2}(\alpha-\beta)=1-c^{2}\), and expand the required expression:
\(\sin^{2}(\alpha-\beta)+2ab\cos(\alpha-\beta)=1-c^{2}+2abc\)
\(=1-(ab+s)^{2}+2ab(ab+s)\)
\(=1-\big(a^{2}b^{2}+2abs+s^{2}\big)+2a^{2}b^{2}+2abs\).
The terms \(-2abs\) and \(+2abs\) cancel, and \(-a^{2}b^{2}+2a^{2}b^{2}=a^{2}b^{2}\), leaving
\(=1+a^{2}b^{2}-s^{2}\).

Step 4 — substitute \(s^{2}\) from Step 2:
\(=1+a^{2}b^{2}-\big(1-a^{2}-b^{2}+a^{2}b^{2}\big)=1+a^{2}b^{2}-1+a^{2}+b^{2}-a^{2}b^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\).

Only \(s^{2}\) ever appears, so the unknown sign of \(\sin u\sin v\) does not affect the answer.

Hence (A).

why: The old solution described a rotation it never carried out, produced a garbled half-computed coordinate pair, and then trailed off into asserting the answer.
solution:
Let \(P=(-1,-1)\) and \(Q=(-\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3})\).

Step 1 — find the side length. 
\(PQ^{2}=(-\sqrt{3}+1)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2}=(3-2\sqrt{3}+1)+(3+2\sqrt{3}+1)=(4-2\sqrt{3})+(4+2\sqrt{3})=8\),
so \(PQ=2\sqrt{2}\).

Step 2 — the third vertex \(R\) must satisfy \(RP^{2}=RQ^{2}=8\). Compute \(RP^{2}\) for each option:

\((-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})\): \(RP^{2}=(-\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}=(3-2\sqrt{2})+(3+2\sqrt{2})=6\neq 8\).

\((\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2})\): \(RP^{2}=(\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}+(-\sqrt{2}+1)^{2}=(3+2\sqrt{2})+(3-2\sqrt{2})=6\neq 8\).

\((1,-1)\): \(RP^{2}=(1+1)^{2}+(-1+1)^{2}=4+0=4\neq 8\).

\((1,1)\): \(RP^{2}=(1+1)^{2}+(1+1)^{2}=4+4=8\) — this one survives.

Step 3 — confirm the surviving point against \(Q\) as well:
\(RQ^{2}=(1+\sqrt{3})^{2}+(1-\sqrt{3})^{2}=(1+2\sqrt{3}+3)+(1-2\sqrt{3}+3)=(4+2\sqrt{3})+(4-2\sqrt{3})=8\).

So for \(R=(1,1)\), \(RP=RQ=PQ=2\sqrt{2}\): all three sides are equal and the triangle is equilateral. (An equilateral triangle on \(PQ\) has two possible third vertices, one on each side of \(PQ\); the question asks only where the third vertex may lie, so exhibiting this one settles it.)

Hence (C).

why: The old solution reached for cube roots of unity and cited a numerical check as its justification; the answer follows directly from the equation itself in two lines.
solution:
Expand the equation: \(x(x+1)+1=x^{2}+x+1=0\).

Since \(k\) is a root, \(k^{2}+k+1=0\), which rearranges to
\(k^{2}=-(k+1)\).

The sum of the two roots of \(x^{2}+x+1=0\) is \(-\dfrac{1}{1}=-1\), so if one root is \(k\) the other is
\(-1-k=-(k+1)\).

Comparing the two displayed lines, the other root \(-(k+1)\) is precisely \(k^{2}\).

A cross-check with the product of roots: the product is \(\dfrac{1}{1}=1\), and \(k\cdot k^{2}=k^{3}\); multiplying \(k^{2}+k+1=0\) by \((k-1)\) gives \(k^{3}-1=0\), so \(k^{3}=1\), as required. Note also \(k\neq 0\), since \(0^{2}+0+1=1\neq 0\), so \(k\) and \(k^{2}\) are genuinely the two roots.

Hence (C).

why: The old solution set up the discriminant correctly but replaced the expansion and the recognition of the perfect square with 'Expanding and simplifying gives'.
solution:
Collect the \(x\) terms:
\(x^{2}-ax-bx-cx+bc+ca=x^{2}-(a+b+c)x+(bc+ca)=0\).

Equal roots means the discriminant is zero:
\((a+b+c)^{2}-4(bc+ca)=0\).

Expand \((a+b+c)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab+2bc+2ca\) and subtract \(4bc+4ca\):
\(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab+2bc+2ca-4bc-4ca=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab-2bc-2ca\).

This is a perfect square. Expanding \((a+b-c)^{2}\) gives
\(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2ab-2ac-2bc\),
which matches the previous line term for term.

So the condition is \((a+b-c)^{2}=0\), and since a square vanishes only when its base does,
\(a+b-c=0\).

Hence (C).

why: The old solution described the permutation loosely and then leaned on a numerical spot-check; the sign is now obtained by counting interchanges explicitly.
solution:
A determinant is unchanged by transposition, so transpose first:
\(\begin{vmatrix} a_{21} & a_{31} & a_{11} \\ a_{23} & a_{33} & a_{13} \\ a_{22} & a_{32} & a_{12} \end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} a_{21} & a_{23} & a_{22} \\ a_{31} & a_{33} & a_{32} \\ a_{11} & a_{13} & a_{12} \end{vmatrix}\)

Read the transposed array against \(A\). Its three rows are rows 2, 3, 1 of \(A\), and within every row the columns stand in the order 1, 3, 2. So it is \(A\) with one row rearrangement and one column rearrangement.

Rows: to go from the order \((1,2,3)\) to \((2,3,1)\), interchange \(R_1\leftrightarrow R_2\) to get \((2,1,3)\), then \(R_2\leftrightarrow R_3\) to get \((2,3,1)\). Two interchanges contribute \((-1)^2=+1\).

Columns: the order \((1,3,2)\) comes from \((1,2,3)\) by the single interchange \(C_2\leftrightarrow C_3\), contributing \(-1\).

Therefore the determinant equals \((+1)(-1)\Delta=-\Delta\).

Hence (D).

why: The old solution quoted \(I_2=\pi/\sqrt{2}\) without proof and asserted \(I_1=\frac{\pi}{2}I_2\); both steps are now derived.
solution:
Step 1 — strip the \(x\) out of \(I_1\). Apply \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx\) with \(a=\pi\), using \(\cos^2(\pi-x)=\cos^2x\):
\(I_1=\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi-x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx\).
Add this to the original expression for \(I_1\):
\(2I_1=\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx\), so \(I_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2}J\) where \(J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{dx}{1+\cos^2x}\).

Step 2 — evaluate \(J\). Since \(\cos^2(\pi-x)=\cos^2x\), the integrand is symmetric about \(x=\pi/2\), so \(J=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\cos^2x}\). Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^2x\) and use \(\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x\):
\(J=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\sec^2x+1}\,dx=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{2+\tan^2x}\,dx\).
Put \(t=\tan x\), \(dt=\sec^2x\,dx\); as \(x:0\to\pi/2\), \(t:0\to\infty\):
\(J=2\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{dt}{2+t^2}=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{\sqrt2}\right]_0^{\infty}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt2}\).

Step 3 — combine. \(I_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\pi^2}{2\sqrt2}\), so \(I_1^2=\dfrac{\pi^4}{4\cdot2}=\dfrac{\pi^4}{8}\) and \(8I_1^2=\pi^4\).

Hence (D).

why: The old solution quoted the value of the integral outright; the substitution that produces it is now shown.
solution:
Because \(\sin^2(\pi-x)=\sin^2x\), the integrand is symmetric about \(x=\pi/2\), so
\(I_2=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\sin^2x}\).

Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^2x\), and use \(\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x\) so that \(\sec^2x+\tan^2x=1+2\tan^2x\):
\(I_2=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\sec^2x+\tan^2x}\,dx=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sec^2x}{1+2\tan^2x}\,dx\).

Put \(t=\tan x\), so \(dt=\sec^2x\,dx\) and the limits \(x:0\to\pi/2\) become \(t:0\to\infty\):
\(I_2=2\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{dt}{1+2t^2}=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt2\,t\right)\right]_0^{\infty}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt2}\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution mis-stated the rationalisation, left a surd expansion unfinished and closed with a numerical check; the product is now factorised into perfect squares so the root is exact.
solution:
For \((3+2\sqrt2)x^2-(4+2\sqrt3)x+(8+4\sqrt3)=0\), the product of the roots is
\(\alpha\beta=\dfrac{8+4\sqrt3}{3+2\sqrt2}\), and the GM is \(\sqrt{\alpha\beta}\).

Write both parts as perfect squares:
\(8+4\sqrt3=2\left(4+2\sqrt3\right)=2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)^2\), since \(\left(\sqrt3+1\right)^2=3+2\sqrt3+1=4+2\sqrt3\);
\(3+2\sqrt2=\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2\), since \(\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2=2+2\sqrt2+1=3+2\sqrt2\).

So \(\alpha\beta=\dfrac{2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)^2}{\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^2}\) and
\(\text{GM}=\sqrt{\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{\sqrt2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)}{\sqrt2+1}\).

Rationalise the denominator: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2+1}=\dfrac{\sqrt2-1}{(\sqrt2+1)(\sqrt2-1)}=\sqrt2-1\). Hence
\(\text{GM}=\sqrt2\left(\sqrt3+1\right)\left(\sqrt2-1\right)\).

Expand the bracket product: \(\left(\sqrt3+1\right)\left(\sqrt2-1\right)=\sqrt6-\sqrt3+\sqrt2-1\), so
\(\text{GM}=\sqrt2\left(\sqrt6-\sqrt3+\sqrt2-1\right)\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution jumped from the substitution to a quadratic in \(s\) that does not follow, then quoted a root; the elimination between \(s\) and \(\sin 2x\) is now carried out in full.
solution:
Put \(s=\sin x+\cos x\) and \(S=\sin 2x=2\sin x\cos x\). Squaring \(s\) gives \(s^2=1+2\sin x\cos x=1+S\), and \(\sin x\cos x=\dfrac{S}{2}\).

Collect the four reciprocal terms over \(\sin x\cos x\):
\(\tan x+\cot x=\dfrac{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}=\dfrac{1}{\sin x\cos x}=\dfrac{2}{S}\),
\(\sec x+\operatorname{cosec} x=\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x\cos x}=\dfrac{2s}{S}\).

The given equation becomes \(s+\dfrac{2}{S}+\dfrac{2s}{S}=7\). Multiply through by \(S\), which is legitimate since \(S=\sin 2x=0\) would leave \(\tan x,\cot x,\sec x,\operatorname{cosec} x\) undefined:
\(sS+2+2s=7S\Rightarrow s(S+2)=7S-2\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{7S-2}{S+2}\).

Now eliminate \(s\) using \(s^2=1+S\):
\((7S-2)^2=(1+S)(S+2)^2\).
Left side: \(49S^2-28S+4\).
Right side: \((1+S)(S^2+4S+4)=S^2+4S+4+S^3+4S^2+4S=S^3+5S^2+8S+4\).
Subtracting,
\(S^3+5S^2+8S+4-49S^2+28S-4=0\Rightarrow S^3-44S^2+36S=0\Rightarrow S\left(S^2-44S+36\right)=0\).

Discarding \(S=0\), the equation reduces to \(\sin^2 2x-44\sin 2x+36=0\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution skipped the equal-tangent step and quoted a quadratic \(m^2-16m-36=0\) that does not come from its own cosine-rule line; the algebra is now done and it factors far more simply.
solution:
The two tangents drawn to a circle from an external point are equal, so at each vertex the two touch-lengths agree:
\(PN=PM=n\), \(QL=QN=n+2\), \(RM=RL=n+4\).

Therefore
\(PQ=PN+NQ=n+(n+2)=2n+2\),
\(PR=PM+MR=n+(n+4)=2n+4\),
\(QR=QL+LR=(n+2)+(n+4)=2n+6\).

Apply the cosine rule at \(P\), the angle opposite \(QR\):
\(\cos P=\dfrac{PQ^2+PR^2-QR^2}{2\cdot PQ\cdot PR}\).

Numerator: \((2n+2)^2+(2n+4)^2-(2n+6)^2=(4n^2+8n+4)+(4n^2+16n+16)-(4n^2+24n+36)=4n^2-16=4(n-2)(n+2)\).
Denominator: \(2(2n+2)(2n+4)=2\cdot2(n+1)\cdot2(n+2)=8(n+1)(n+2)\).

So \(\cos P=\dfrac{4(n-2)(n+2)}{8(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac{n-2}{2(n+1)}\).

Set this equal to \(\dfrac13\):
\(3(n-2)=2(n+1)\Rightarrow 3n-6=2n+2\Rightarrow n=8\).

The sides are then \(18,20,22\), and \(\cos P=\dfrac{18^2+20^2-22^2}{2(18)(20)}=\dfrac{240}{720}=\dfrac13\); \(QR=22\) is the longest side, so \(P\) is indeed the largest angle, as the question requires.

Hence (C).

why: The old solution stalled at \(A=\pi/2\) (a wrong deduction) and then quoted the answer; the condition in fact reduces to \(A=|B-C|\), and the branch giving a determinate value is identified explicitly.
solution:
First simplify what is asked:
\(\tan\dfrac B2+\cot\dfrac B2=\dfrac{\sin^2(B/2)+\cos^2(B/2)}{\sin(B/2)\cos(B/2)}=\dfrac{1}{\tfrac12\sin B}=\dfrac{2}{\sin B}\).

Now use the given condition. Since \(A+B+C=\pi\), we have \(\dfrac{B+C}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac A2\), so \(\cos\dfrac{B+C}{2}=\sin\dfrac A2\) and
\(\cos B+\cos C=2\cos\dfrac{B+C}{2}\cos\dfrac{B-C}{2}=2\sin\dfrac A2\cos\dfrac{B-C}{2}\),
while \(\sin A=2\sin\dfrac A2\cos\dfrac A2\).

Equating the two sides of \(\sin A=\cos B+\cos C\) and cancelling \(\sin\dfrac A2\), which is non-zero for \(0<A<\pi\):
\(\cos\dfrac A2=\cos\dfrac{B-C}{2}\).
Both \(\dfrac A2\) and \(\dfrac{B-C}{2}\) lie in \(\left(-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right)\), where cosine is one-to-one on magnitudes, so \(A=|B-C|\).

Take \(A=B-C\). Then \(B=A+C\), and substituting into \(A+B+C=\pi\) gives \(B+B=\pi\), so \(B=\dfrac\pi2\) and \(\sin B=1\). Therefore
\(\tan\dfrac B2+\cot\dfrac B2=\dfrac{2}{\sin B}=2\).

Hence (D).

[Note on the other branch: \(A=C-B\) forces \(C=\dfrac\pi2\) and leaves \(B\) free, so \(2/\sin B\) is then not a fixed number and matches none of the four options (for example \(A=60^\circ,B=30^\circ,C=90^\circ\) satisfies the given condition and gives \(4\)). The configuration intended by the question is the right angle at \(B\).]

why: The old solution asserted the two component integrals equal \(\pi/4\); the pairing argument that establishes it is now shown.
solution:
Split the numerator and write
\(J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\), \(\;K=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\), so that \(k=\dfrac{aJ+bK}{a+b}\).

Adding the two integrals:
\(J+K=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}dx=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

The two are also equal. Apply \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx\) to \(J\) with \(a=\dfrac\pi2\), using \(\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\cos x\) and \(\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\sin x\):
\(J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x+\sin x}\,dx=K\).

So \(2J=\dfrac\pi2\), giving \(J=K=\dfrac\pi4\), and therefore
\(k=\dfrac{a\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}+b\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}}{a+b}=\dfrac{(a+b)\frac{\pi}{4}}{a+b}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Hence (A).

why: The old solution wandered through fractional powers and a special case before stumbling onto the answer; parametrising the GP by its common ratio settles it in two lines.
solution:
Let the common ratio of the GP \(p,\;g_1,\;g_2,\;q\) be \(r\). Then
\(g_1=pr\), \(g_2=pr^2\), \(q=pr^3\).

So
\(\dfrac{g_1^2}{g_2}=\dfrac{p^2r^2}{pr^2}=p\), and \(\dfrac{g_2^2}{g_1}=\dfrac{p^2r^4}{pr}=pr^3=q\).

Adding, \(\dfrac{g_1^2}{g_2}+\dfrac{g_2^2}{g_1}=p+q\).

Since \(m\) is the arithmetic mean of \(p\) and \(q\), \(m=\dfrac{p+q}{2}\), so \(p+q=2m\).

Hence (B).

why: The old solution trailed off mid-identity twice and then asserted the value; the numerator and denominator are now each reduced to \(\sin 40^\circ\) so the ratio is exact.
solution:
\(\dfrac{\sqrt3\,p}{4}-\dfrac{q}{4}=\dfrac14\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sin 20^\circ}-\dfrac{1}{\sin 70^\circ}\right)=\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3\sin 70^\circ-\sin 20^\circ}{\sin 20^\circ\sin 70^\circ}\).

Use \(\sin 70^\circ=\cos 20^\circ\) throughout.

Numerator: \(\sqrt3\cos 20^\circ-\sin 20^\circ=2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos 20^\circ-\dfrac12\sin 20^\circ\right)=2\left(\sin 60^\circ\cos 20^\circ-\cos 60^\circ\sin 20^\circ\right)\).
By \(\sin(X-Y)=\sin X\cos Y-\cos X\sin Y\), this is \(2\sin\left(60^\circ-20^\circ\right)=2\sin 40^\circ\).

Denominator: \(\sin 20^\circ\cos 20^\circ=\dfrac12\left(2\sin 20^\circ\cos 20^\circ\right)=\dfrac12\sin 40^\circ\).

Therefore
\(\dfrac{\sqrt3\,p}{4}-\dfrac{q}{4}=\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac{2\sin 40^\circ}{\tfrac12\sin 40^\circ}=\dfrac14\times 4=1\).

Hence (C).

why: The old solution declared its own working 'complex', abandoned it and asserted the answer as a standard result; the deduction is actually two clean Vieta steps once the log is inverted by change of base.
solution:
Write \(t=\log_{0.5}(a^2)\), so \(t>0\) and the equation is \(x^2+tx+t^4=0\).
By the change-of-base rule \(\log_{a^2}(0.5)=\dfrac{1}{\log_{0.5}(a^2)}=\dfrac{1}{t}\), so the given condition \(\beta^2=\alpha\log_{a^2}(0.5)\) reads
\(\beta^2=\dfrac{\alpha}{t}\), i.e. \(\alpha=t\beta^2\).
Vieta's relations for \(x^2+tx+t^4=0\) give \(\alpha+\beta=-t\) and \(\alpha\beta=t^4\).
Put \(\alpha=t\beta^2\) into the product:
\(t\beta^2\cdot\beta=t^4\Rightarrow t\beta^3=t^4\Rightarrow\beta^3=t^3\Rightarrow\beta=t\).
Now use the sum:
\(\alpha=-t-\beta=-t-t=-2t\), and since \(\beta=t\) this is \(\alpha=-2\beta\).
Hence (C).

why: The old solution broke off mid-expansion with an ellipsis and asserted the cross terms sum to 6ab; every square is now expanded and the two cube-root identities applied visibly.
solution:
The non-real cube roots of unity satisfy \(\omega^3=1\) and \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\); consequently \(\omega^4=\omega^3\cdot\omega=\omega\).
Square each of the three expressions.
\(x^2=(a+b)^2=a^2+b^2+2ab\).
\(y^2=(a\omega+b\omega^2)^2=a^2\omega^2+b^2\omega^4+2ab\,\omega^3=a^2\omega^2+b^2\omega+2ab\).
\(z^2=(a\omega^2+b\omega)^2=a^2\omega^4+b^2\omega^2+2ab\,\omega^3=a^2\omega+b^2\omega^2+2ab\).
Add the three, grouping the \(a^2\) terms and the \(b^2\) terms:
\(x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2(1+\omega^2+\omega)+b^2(1+\omega+\omega^2)+6ab\).
Both brackets are \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\), so
\(x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2\cdot 0+b^2\cdot 0+6ab=6ab\).
Hence (A).

why: The old solution quoted the two closed-form antiderivatives without producing them; one integration by parts gives the relation directly and needs no closed form at all.
solution:
By the fundamental theorem of calculus, differentiating each integral returns its integrand:
\(\dfrac{du}{dx}=e^x\cos x\) and \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}=e^x\sin x\).
Now integrate \(v\) by parts, taking \(\sin x\) as the first function and \(e^x\) as the second:
\(v=\int e^x\sin x\,dx=\sin x\cdot e^x-\int(\cos x)e^x\,dx=e^x\sin x-\int e^x\cos x\,dx\).
The integral that remains is exactly \(u\), so \(v=e^x\sin x-u\), that is
\(u+v=e^x\sin x\).
Comparing with \(\dfrac{dv}{dx}=e^x\sin x\) gives \(u+v=\dfrac{dv}{dx}\).
Hence (D).

why: The old solution set up the tangent formula and then asserted that substituting 'simplifies to tan(theta)=1' without doing the algebra; the whole cancellation is now shown.
solution:
Put both lines in the form \(Ax+By=C\) and read off their normal vectors.
First line: \(px+qy=p+q\), normal \(\vec{n_1}=(p,\,q)\).
Second line: \(p(x-y)+q(x+y)=2q\Rightarrow (p+q)x+(q-p)y=2q\), normal \(\vec{n_2}=(p+q,\,q-p)\).
The acute angle between two lines equals the acute angle between their normals.
Dot product: \(\vec{n_1}\cdot\vec{n_2}=p(p+q)+q(q-p)=p^2+pq+q^2-pq=p^2+q^2\).
Lengths: \(|\vec{n_1}|=\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\) and
\(|\vec{n_2}|=\sqrt{(p+q)^2+(q-p)^2}=\sqrt{p^2+2pq+q^2+q^2-2pq+p^2}=\sqrt{2(p^2+q^2)}\).
Therefore
\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{p^2+q^2}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\cdot\sqrt{2(p^2+q^2)}}=\dfrac{p^2+q^2}{\sqrt2\,(p^2+q^2)}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\).
So \(\theta=45^\circ\), and \(\sin\theta=\sin45^\circ=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\).
Hence (D).

why: The old solution wrote the correct reciprocal-AP condition and then jumped straight to b^2=ac; the cross-multiplication and cancellation are now carried out.
solution:
If \((a+b),\,2b,\,(b+c)\) are in HP, then their reciprocals \(\dfrac{1}{a+b},\ \dfrac{1}{2b},\ \dfrac{1}{b+c}\) are in AP, so twice the middle term equals the sum of the outer two:
\(\dfrac{2}{2b}=\dfrac{1}{a+b}+\dfrac{1}{b+c}\), i.e. \(\dfrac{1}{b}=\dfrac{(b+c)+(a+b)}{(a+b)(b+c)}=\dfrac{a+2b+c}{(a+b)(b+c)}\).
Cross-multiplying: \((a+b)(b+c)=b(a+2b+c)\).
Expand each side:
left \(=ab+ac+b^2+bc\), right \(=ab+2b^2+bc\).
Cancel \(ab+bc\) from both sides: \(ac+b^2=2b^2\), so \(b^2=ac\).
Thus \(b\) is the geometric mean of \(a\) and \(c\), i.e. \(a,\,b,\,c\) are in GP.
Hence (C).

why: The old solution asserted that cross-multiplying 'simplifies to 2a=d' with none of the algebra, and also dropped the p/q factor when forming the ratio without saying so.
solution:
For an AP, \(S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a+(n-1)d\big]\), so
\(\dfrac{S_p}{S_q}=\dfrac{p\big[2a+(p-1)d\big]}{q\big[2a+(q-1)d\big]}=\dfrac{p^2}{q^2}\).
Cancel one factor \(\dfrac{p}{q}\) from both sides:
\(\dfrac{2a+(p-1)d}{2a+(q-1)d}=\dfrac{p}{q}\).
Cross-multiply:
\(q\big[2a+(p-1)d\big]=p\big[2a+(q-1)d\big]\)
\(\Rightarrow 2aq+pqd-qd=2ap+pqd-pd\).
The term \(pqd\) cancels from both sides, leaving
\(2aq-qd=2ap-pd\)
\(\Rightarrow 2a(q-p)=d(q-p)\).
The ratio condition is stated for \(p\neq q\), so \(q-p\neq0\) and we may divide by it:
\(d=2a\).
That is, the common difference equals twice the first term.
Hence (C).

why: The old solution offered two half-started routes and then asserted the value; the half-angle reduction plus one sum-to-product step is now carried through to the cancellation.
solution:
First, \(\sin(-95^\circ)=-\sin95^\circ=-\sin(90^\circ+5^\circ)=-\cos5^\circ\), so \(r^2=\cos^2 5^\circ\) and
\(p^2+q^2+r^2=\sin^2 35^\circ+\sin^2 25^\circ+\cos^2 5^\circ\).
Apply \(\sin^2\phi=\dfrac{1-\cos2\phi}{2}\) to the first two and \(\cos^2\phi=\dfrac{1+\cos2\phi}{2}\) to the third:
\(=\dfrac{1-\cos70^\circ}{2}+\dfrac{1-\cos50^\circ}{2}+\dfrac{1+\cos10^\circ}{2}=\dfrac{3-(\cos70^\circ+\cos50^\circ)+\cos10^\circ}{2}\).
Combine the bracket by the sum-to-product identity \(\cos A+\cos B=2\cos\dfrac{A+B}{2}\cos\dfrac{A-B}{2}\):
\(\cos70^\circ+\cos50^\circ=2\cos60^\circ\cos10^\circ=2\cdot\dfrac12\cdot\cos10^\circ=\cos10^\circ\).
So the numerator becomes \(3-\cos10^\circ+\cos10^\circ=3\), and
\(p^2+q^2+r^2=\dfrac{3}{2}\).
Hence (C).

why: The old solution quoted the point-of-contact formula (a/m^2, 2a/m) as a given; for this parabola the point falls out of two lines of implicit differentiation, so the formula need not be assumed.
solution:
The tangent makes \(45^\circ\) with the positive \(x\)-axis, so its slope is \(\tan45^\circ=1\).
Differentiate \(y^2=4x\) implicitly with respect to \(x\):
\(2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{y}\).
At the point of contact \((x_1,y_1)\) this derivative is the slope of the tangent:
\(\dfrac{2}{y_1}=1\Rightarrow y_1=2\).
The point of contact lies on the parabola, so \(y_1^2=4x_1\):
\(4=4x_1\Rightarrow x_1=1\).
The point of contact is \((1,\,2)\).
Hence (D).
